title: Build Logic with Pseudocode and Decomposition
learningObjectives: Translate a problem statement into language-neutral pseudocode steps
Decompose a large algorithm into focused reusable methods
Define method inputs, outputs and observable behavior clearly
Trace sample data through each algorithm step systematically
State invariants that should remain true during processing

understand.concept: Pseudocode describes an algorithm without Java syntax. Decompose a task into named steps and methods with clear inputs and outputs. Trace a small example and check that each step preserves the intended invariant.
understand.whyItMatters: Build Logic with Pseudocode and Decomposition helps learners create Java applications that are easier to reason about, test and maintain. It connects core language knowledge with realistic programming tasks.

explain.narrative:
## Build Logic with Pseudocode and Decomposition

Pseudocode describes an algorithm without Java syntax. Decompose a task into named steps and methods with clear inputs and outputs. Trace a small example and check that each step preserves the intended invariant.

## Applying the concept

Identify the input and desired result. Select the Java construct or API that directly supports the requirement. Keep code readable, handle documented failure cases and state assumptions clearly.

## Verification checklist

- Compile with JDK 21.
- Predict the output before running.
- Test normal, boundary and invalid inputs where relevant.
- Check resource cleanup and error handling.
- Prefer explicit types and focused methods.

examples.title: Core concept
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int subtotal = 200; int tax = subtotal / 10; System.out.println(subtotal + tax); } }
examples.explanation: Calculates a subtotal, tax amount and final total.

examples.title: Practical use
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int[] values = {2, 4, 6}; int sum = 0; for (int value : values) sum += value; System.out.println(sum); } }
examples.explanation: Decomposes aggregation into initialization, traversal and accumulation.

examples.title: Boundary behavior
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.function.IntUnaryOperator doubleValue = value -> value * 2; System.out.println(doubleValue.applyAsInt(7)); } }
examples.explanation: Extracts a focused operation into a reusable functional value.

examples.title: Alternative pattern
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int balance = 100; int withdrawal = 30; if (withdrawal <= balance) balance -= withdrawal; System.out.println(balance); } }
examples.explanation: Preserves an invariant: a withdrawal cannot exceed the available balance.

examples.title: Verify the result
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String[] steps = {"read", "validate", "calculate", "display"}; for (int i=0; i<steps.length; i++) System.out.println((i+1)+". "+steps[i]); } }
examples.explanation: Represents an algorithm as ordered steps before implementing each step.

practise.guidedTask: Write pseudocode for finding the second-largest distinct number. Trace it using a normal list, duplicates and a one-element list, then translate it into Java methods.
practise.independentTask: Decompose a student-report problem into input parsing, validation, calculation and formatting methods. Define each method's inputs and output.
hints: Break the work into small methods with clear inputs and outputs.
Validate data before calculating or changing stored state.
Compile with JDK 21 and compare actual results with your test table.
practise.challenge: Extend the algorithm with an invariant that explains why the current largest and second-largest values remain correct after each iteration.
